d: How close a measurement is to the true value of the quantity being measured.
How closely a set of repeated measurements agree with each other.
The closeness of agreement of results when the same person repeats the measurement with the same method and equipment under the same conditions.
The closeness of agreement of results when the measurement is carried out by different people, or with different equipment or in a different laboratory.
Whether an experiment and its measurements actually test what they are intended to test.
An error that causes readings to differ from the true value by a consistent amount each time, affecting accuracy.
An unpredictable variation in measurements that affects precision and is reduced by repeating and averaging.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
The weighted mean of the relative isotopic masses of an element, on a scale where carbon-12 is exactly 12.
The ability of an atom to attract electrons in a covalent bond towards itself.
The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of atoms in the gaseous state.
The attractive force felt by valence electrons: the number of protons minus the number of inner-shell electrons.
The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ specified particles.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
A substance that donates a proton (H⁺) to another substance.
A substance that accepts a proton (H⁺) from another substance.
Able to act as either an acid or a base, by donating or accepting a proton.
An acid that ionises completely in water.
Loss of electrons; an increase in oxidation number.
Gain of electrons; a decrease in oxidation number.
A substance that causes another to be oxidised and is itself reduced.
A substance that causes another to be reduced and is itself oxidised.
A solution of accurately known concentration.
A substance pure and stable enough to be weighed out to make a solution of accurately known concentration.
The point in a titration when the reactants have been mixed in the mole ratio shown by the balanced equation.
The point in a titration when the indicator changes colour.
The reactant that is completely consumed in a reaction and so determines the amount of product.
A temperature of 25 °C and a pressure of 100 kPa.
A reaction that releases energy to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.
The minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, without being consumed.
The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the system adjusts to partially oppose the effect of the change.
A cell that converts chemical energy to electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction.
A cell that uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
A galvanic cell that produces electricity continuously while reactants are supplied.
Compounds with the same molecular formula and different structural formulas.
A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.
The percentage of the total mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product.
The design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances.
A system in which materials are kept in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, in contrast to a take–make–dispose linear economy.
A change in the shape of a protein caused by disruption of its secondary, tertiary or quaternary structure, without breaking peptide links.
The time a component takes to pass through a chromatography column.
The level of formality of a text, on a scale from informal to formal, chosen to suit the context.
The relationship between the participants in a text, including social distance and relative status.
The subject matter or topic of a text.
The channel of communication: spoken, written or signed, including digital forms.
The immediate circumstances of a text: field, language mode, setting, text type and the relationship between participants.
The values, attitudes and beliefs held by the participants and the wider community that influence a text.
Language used to create and maintain social contact, not to pass on information.
The smallest unit of meaning in a language. Free morphemes stand alone; bound morphemes must attach to another morpheme.
A bound morpheme that marks grammatical information such as tense or number without changing word class.
A bound morpheme that creates a new word or changes word class.
Forming a noun from a verb or adjective, such as “decision” from “decide”.
Leaving out words that can be recovered from the context.
The linguistic ties that link parts of a text, such as reference, repetition, conjunctions and ellipsis.
The way a text makes sense as a whole to its audience, through logical ordering, consistency, formatting, inference and conventions.
A word that points back to something mentioned earlier in the text.
A word that points forward to something mentioned later in the text.
A word or phrase that organises talk or signals the speaker’s attitude, such as “well”, “so” or “anyway”.
Two related turns by different speakers, where the first expects the second, such as question and answer.
A person’s need to be liked, approved of and included.
A person’s need to act freely and not be imposed upon.
An utterance that risks damaging the positive or negative face of the speaker or the listener.
Status given publicly to standard forms of a language.
Status that non-standard forms have within a particular group.
A mild or indirect expression used in place of one considered unpleasant or taboo.
A harsh or blunt expression used in place of a neutral one.
Language that deliberately disguises, distorts or reverses the meaning of words.
The specialised vocabulary of a profession or interest group.
Informal, often short-lived vocabulary associated with a particular group.
The language variety unique to an individual.
A language variety associated with a social group, such as an age group or occupation.
A variety of a language associated with an ethnic or cultural group, influenced by a heritage language.
The variety of Australian English that is codified and used in education, government, the law and the media.
Moving between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation.
A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language. It has no native speakers.
A language that developed from a pidgin and is acquired by children as a first language.
The view that some language forms are correct and should be enforced.
The approach of describing how language is used without judging it.
A child’s application of a regular grammatical rule to an irregular case, such as “goed”.
The systematic, developing language of someone learning an additional language.
Rising intonation at the end of a statement, common in Australian English.
The records of the assets, liabilities and business activities of the entity are kept completely separate from those of the owner and of other entities.
Financial reports are prepared on the assumption that the business will continue to operate in the future.
The life of the business is divided into periods of time so that reports can be prepared and performance measured for each period.
Revenues are recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, so that profit is calculated as revenue earned in a period less expenses incurred in that period.
Financial information is relevant if it is capable of making a difference to the decisions made by users.
Financial information should be complete, neutral (free from bias) and free from material error.
Different knowledgeable and independent observers could reach agreement that the information is faithfully represented, for example by checking source documents.
Users can identify similarities and differences between reports of different periods or different businesses, which requires consistent accounting methods.
Financial information is available to decision-makers in time to be capable of influencing their decisions.
Financial information is classified, characterised and presented clearly and concisely.
A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events.
A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events.
The residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all its liabilities.
An increase in assets or a decrease in liabilities that results in an increase in owner’s equity, other than a contribution from the owner.
A decrease in assets or an increase in liabilities that results in a decrease in owner’s equity, other than a distribution to the owner (drawings).
An asset expected to be sold, consumed or converted to cash within 12 months.
An asset expected to be used by the business for more than 12 months.
The written or electronic evidence of a transaction, used to record it.
The allocation of the depreciable amount of a non-current asset over its useful life.
The cost of a non-current asset less its accumulated depreciation.
The estimated selling price of inventory less the estimated costs of selling, marketing and distributing it.
A cost incurred to bring inventory into a condition and location ready for sale that can be allocated to individual units on a logical basis.
A cost incurred to bring inventory into a condition and location ready for sale that cannot be allocated to individual units on a logical basis.
The cost price of the inventory sold in a period.
An expense recognised when the physical count of inventory is less than the balance shown on the inventory card.
An entry made at the end of a period so that revenue accounts show revenue earned and expense accounts show expenses incurred in that period.
An expense incurred in the period but not yet paid: a current liability.
An amount paid for goods or services not yet consumed: a current asset.
Cash received for goods or services not yet provided: a current liability.
Revenue earned in the period but not yet received: a current asset.
The process of predicting the financial consequences of future events.
The difference between an actual figure and the budgeted figure, described as favourable or unfavourable.
The ability of the business to earn profit, measured by comparing profit against a base such as sales, assets or owner’s equity.
The ability of the business to meet its short-term debts as they fall due.
The ability of the business to meet its debts and continue operating in the long term.
The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so that profit is zero.
A relation in which each element of the domain is paired with exactly one element of the range.
The set of all values of the independent variable for which a function is defined.
The set of all values a function takes.
A function in which each element of the range is the image of exactly one element of the domain.
The function \(f^{-1}\) that reverses a one-to-one function \(f\), so that \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\).
A function formed by applying one function to the result of another: \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\).
A line that a graph approaches but does not reach as \(x\) or \(y\) becomes very large.
A transformation that stretches or compresses a graph by a factor from an axis.
The horizontal length of one complete cycle of a periodic function.
Half the distance between the maximum and minimum values of a circular function.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function; the gradient of the tangent to its graph at a point.
A point on a graph where the derivative is zero.
A point on a graph where the concavity changes.
A function \(F\) whose derivative is the given function \(f\).
\(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)\), the signed area between the graph of \(f\) and the \(x\)-axis from \(a\) to \(b\).
\(\dfrac{1}{b - a}\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) over the interval \([a, b]\).
Events that cannot occur together: \(\Pr(A \cap B) = 0\).
Events for which \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A) \times \Pr(B)\).
The probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) has occurred: \(\Pr(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)}\).
A random variable whose possible values can be listed.
The long-run mean of a random variable: \(\operatorname{E}(X) = \sum x\Pr(X = x)\) for a discrete variable.
The distribution of the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials, each with the same probability \(p\) of success.
A function \(f\) with \(f(x) \ge 0\) and total area 1, where areas under the graph give probabilities for a continuous random variable.
The proportion of a sample with a particular attribute, \(\hat{p}\), used to estimate the population proportion \(p\).
An interval calculated from a sample that, for a stated percentage of samples, contains the population parameter.
The distance from the sample proportion to each end of a confidence interval.
A variable whose values are categories. Nominal categories have no order; ordinal categories have a natural order.
A variable whose values are counts or measurements. Discrete values can be listed; continuous values can be any value in an interval.
The middle value of an ordered data set.
The spread of the middle 50% of the data: \(Q_3 - Q_1\).
A value below \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) or above \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\).
A measure of the typical spread of data values around the mean.
The number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean: \(z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\).
The variable used to explain or predict changes in the response variable.
The variable whose changes are explained or predicted by the explanatory variable.
A measure of the strength and direction of a linear association between two numerical variables, from \(-1\) to \(1\).
\(r^2\): the proportion of the variation in the response variable explained by the variation in the explanatory variable.
Actual value minus predicted value.
Predicting within the range of the data.
Predicting outside the range of the data.
The ratio of a season’s value to the average season’s value.
A rule that gives each term of a sequence from the previous term, together with a starting value.
The annual interest rate as quoted, before the effect of compounding within the year.
The annual rate that gives the same interest as the nominal rate with its compounding periods.
A loan on which interest is calculated on the remaining balance and regular payments reduce the balance.
An investment that earns compound interest and from which regular payments are made.
An annuity in which the regular payment equals the interest earned, so it lasts indefinitely.
The process of paying off a loan with regular payments over time.
A square matrix describing the proportions that move from each state to each state in one time period; each column sums to 1.
The long-run state matrix that no longer changes when multiplied by the transition matrix.
The number of edges attached to a vertex, with a loop counted twice.
A trail that includes every edge of a graph exactly once.
A path that visits every vertex of a graph exactly once.
A spanning tree of a weighted graph with the smallest possible total weight.
The cut of a flow network with the smallest capacity; its capacity equals the maximum flow.
The longest path through an activity network; it determines the minimum completion time of the project.
The time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project: latest start time minus earliest start time.
